standard: GDD rework v2 · 80+ researched scenarios · scorecard-passed
note: Recognising & responding (without shame) to a child's substance / screen / gaming dependence; getting help early; modelling healthy habits (UNESCO 5.1, 5.5, 5.6). New v2 build, a high-care Parent Layer pillar. The core insight: shame and punishment drive addiction underground, while calm, connection and the right help bring it into the light. Six modes: spot the signs (warning signs of substance and screen/gaming dependence, what's typical versus concerning, with calm noticing not panic or snooping, and gaming disorder is a recognised condition), respond, don't rupture (bust 'crack down / it's just willpower / good kids don't / shame will scare them straight'; calm, connected responses, connection over control and surveillance, firm about the behaviour and unconditionally there for the child), it's a health issue (dependence is a treatable health condition involving the brain, genes and environment, not weak willpower or a moral failing, and treatment works and recovery is real), get the right help (counselling and de-addiction services early, family involvement strongly improves outcomes, and routes to Tele-MANAS 14416 and Childline 1098), screens and modelling (calm agreed screen limits the whole family keeps, healthy outlets, and honestly examining and tending your own substance and screen habits), tools and safety (a signs-and-help-finder and calm-response plan, and any acute risk such as a possible overdose or danger treated as an emergency to route immediately to 112 or a hospital). High-care and firmly non-shaming of both child and parent, it frames dependence as health not moral failure, never provides any how-to for obtaining or using substances, treats acute risk as an emergency, and is not medical advice, pointing to professionals. Builds on Bounce (g39) and connects to the screen-literacy thread (Reality Check g28, Decoded g36). India: youth substance use and screen/gaming dependence are both rising while stigma and harsh punitive responses are common, exactly what drives the problem deeper, so the node de-stigmatises and signposts real help (counselling, de-addiction centres, Tele-MANAS 14416, Childline 1098).

evidenceBase: Dependence can affect any child and is not a verdict on the child or the parenting: substance dependence and behavioural dependence are both real, gaming disorder is a recognised condition in the WHO ICD-11 (impaired control over gaming, increasing priority over other activities, and continuation despite negative consequences), and screen or phone dependence can genuinely disrupt a child's sleep, mood and life. The warning signs across substances and screens are loss of control, escalation and the disruption of normal life, and they are best read with calm curiosity and the whole picture over time rather than panic, accusation or pure surveillance, because the goal is to reach a child rather than to catch them (WHO adolescent health and ICD-11 gaming disorder)

Shame and punishment drive dependence underground while calm connection keeps a child reachable, and addiction is a treatable health condition rather than a moral failing: harsh crackdowns, threats, humiliation and cutting off connection make a struggling child hide, lie and feel they cannot come to a parent, whereas calm concern, an open door and being firm about the behaviour while unconditionally there for the child keep them safe and willing to accept help. Addiction is a treatable, chronic health condition involving the brain's reward system, genetics and environment, not weak willpower or bad character, so 'just stop' is genuinely hard, recovery is real and common with support, and the stigma of 'bad', 'weak' or 'hopeless' is what most needs to go (addiction-as-treatable-health-condition research; non-punitive, connection-based parenting evidence)

Early professional help with family involvement works, own habits matter, and acute risk is an emergency: dependence usually needs professional help, counsellors and de-addiction services know what works, and family-based involvement strongly improves outcomes (family-inclusive approaches markedly outperform adolescent-only ones), so getting help early, before a crisis, gives the best chance just as with any health issue. Parents also model habits, so calm agreed screen limits the whole family keeps and honestly tending one's own substance and screen habits are part of helping a child, and any acute risk such as a possible overdose or immediate danger is an emergency to route at once to medical help (112 or a hospital). The node is high-care and non-shaming, provides no how-to for substances, and is not medical advice, signposting Tele-MANAS 14416, Childline 1098 and de-addiction services (family-based adolescent treatment research; Tele-MANAS / Childline; WHO)

options.text: Let the judgement colour how you treat them
options.consequence: Separating the child from the condition lets you respond with care; judging them as 'bad' fuels the shame that deepens it.

scenarios.debrief: Separate your child from the condition: they have a health problem, they aren't a bad person.

scenarios.hook: A relative dismisses your child's struggle as 'just being spoilt'. You want to reframe it firmly.
scenarios.relearn: Firmly reframing dependence as a health condition needing treatment protects your child from stigma-driven contempt.

yourLine.text: "It's a real health condition, not spoiling, and what helps is treatment and support, not contempt."
"Maybe you're right, we did spoil him."

scenarios.hook: Spot the belief that supports a child's recovery.
scenarios.relearn: Support recovery with belief that it's treatable and you're in their corner, not 'lost cause' despair.

scene.text: 'This is treatable and you can recover'

scenarios.why: 'Treatable, you can recover' and 'I'm in your corner' support recovery; 'lost cause' destroys the hope it needs.

scenarios.hook: You're nervous about calling a de-addiction service for the first time. You picture how to begin.
scenarios.relearn: A simple, honest opening is all a service needs; you don't need the perfect words to start getting help.

yourLine.text: "Hello, I'm worried my child may be dependent on something, and I want to understand how to help them."
"Sorry, never mind, we'll handle it ourselves somehow."

scenarios.hook: Sort: gets a child effective help, or delays it?
scenarios.relearn: Early professional help and a family-inclusive plan get help; waiting for rock bottom and secrecy delay it.

scenarios.hook: The first help you try doesn't seem to fit your child.
scenarios.relearn: Keep searching for the right-fit help; one poor fit doesn't mean nothing can help your child.

options.text: Keep looking for the right professional or approach
options.consequence: You find the support that works for them.

options.text: Conclude that nothing and no one can help
options.consequence: Persisting to find the right fit gets effective help; concluding nothing helps abandons a child who is treatable.

scenarios.debrief: If the first help doesn't fit, keep looking for the right professional or approach rather than giving up.

scenarios.hook: Match each worry about getting help to the reassuring truth.
scenarios.relearn: Each worry about getting help has a reassurance: it's wise, treatment works, and you're not alone.

pairs.right: It's wise, like any health issue
Treatment helps and recovery is real

scenarios.hook: Your struggling child resists treatment. You want to encourage them without force.
scenarios.relearn: Encouraging with companionship and 'you're not alone' invites a child toward help better than threats and ultimatums.

yourLine.text: "I'll be with you every step, getting help is brave, and you don't have to face this alone."
"Go to rehab or you're out of this house."

scenarios.hook: Spot the move that opens the door to real help.
scenarios.relearn: Open the door to help by reaching out early and involving the family, not hiding it until crisis.
scenarios.why: Reaching out early and involving the family open the door to help; hiding it until crisis closes it.

scenarios.hook: Your child says your phone use is hypocritical when you set their limits. You want to respond with honesty.
scenarios.relearn: Owning the hypocrisy and committing to the same limits gives the rules integrity and models honesty.

yourLine.text: "You're right, and I'm going to follow the same limits, we'll do this together as a family."
"Don't be cheeky, the rules are for you, not me."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a habit that helps a child manage screens, or one that fuels dependence?
scenarios.relearn: Screen-free meals and good offline options help; endless screen time and screens-as-only-coping fuel dependence.

items.text: Screens as the only way to cope

scenarios.hook: You want to reduce your child's gaming but they have nothing else to fill the time.
scenarios.relearn: Fill the gap with better things when cutting screen time; a void just pulls a child back to the habit.

options.text: Replace screen time with appealing offline activities together
options.consequence: You crowd out the habit with better things.

options.text: Just take the device and leave a void
options.consequence: Replacing screen time with appealing activities crowds out the habit; just removing the device leaves a void that pulls them back.

scenarios.debrief: Reduce gaming by replacing it with appealing offline activities, not just removing the device and leaving a void.

scenarios.hook: Match each modelling choice to what it teaches a child.
scenarios.relearn: Parents off phones, healthy de-stressing and owning slip-ups each teach a child something that protects them.

scenarios.hook: You want to set a family tech agreement together rather than imposing rules. You propose it.
scenarios.relearn: Proposing a fair family agreement everyone shapes, parents included, gets far more buy-in than imposed, arbitrary rules.

yourLine.text: "Let's make a family screen plan together, fair for everyone, parents included, what should be in it?"
"New rule: I confiscate phones whenever I feel like it."

scenarios.hook: Sort: models healthy habits, or models the opposite?
scenarios.relearn: Coping without substances and balanced phone use model healthy habits; nightly drinking and doom-scrolling model the opposite.

scenarios.hook: You want to make sure both you and your co-parent know what to do in an emergency. You set the plan.
scenarios.relearn: Agreeing a clear emergency plan in advance means no hesitation when seconds count.

yourLine.text: "If there's ever an emergency, we call 112 or go straight to hospital, no hesitation, agreed?"
"Let's just hope nothing like that ever happens."

scenarios.hook: Sort: a wise preparation, or a risky gap?
scenarios.relearn: Saved numbers and knowing the danger signs are wise; no crisis plan and 'never us' denial are risky gaps.

items.text: Knowing the signs of acute danger
Assuming it'll never happen to you

scenarios.hook: A friend's child is struggling and they don't know where to turn. You want to point them to help.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing that it's a health issue with concrete help routes serves a struggling friend far better than fuelling shame.

yourLine.text: "It's a health issue, not a disgrace, Tele-MANAS 14416 and a de-addiction counsellor are good places to start."
"That's so shameful, I wouldn't tell anyone if I were you."

scenarios.hook: Your child is finally getting help and you want to commit to staying involved. You tell them.
scenarios.relearn: Committing to stay involved through recovery, good days and hard, gives a child the steady support that helps it last.

yourLine.text: "I'm in this with you for the long haul, the good days and the hard ones, you're not alone."
"There, I got you help, now it's your problem to fix."
